title: Two Shuffles, Done Well
description: Overhand and riffle as handling skills: what each does to the order, and how to look relaxed
tryIt: Practise the overhand shuffle with the last-card finish until you can talk through it, then perform Shuffled Prediction for one person at dinner.

concepts.title: How it works: blocks and zips
concepts.contentHtml:
Before any trick, a spectator watches you shuffle and decides in a few seconds whether you look like someone who knows cards. Reginald Scot, who exposed conjurors in 1584, thought it worth ranking: the third principal point of sleight of hand was shuffling the cards,1 after hiding balls and swapping money. So we begin with the two shuffles you will use all through this skill, and with what each one really does to the order.

In the overhand shuffle you peel small packets off the top of the deck in one hand and let each fall on top of the pile in the other. Because every new packet lands on top, the first packet you took finishes at the bottom and the last on top. In effect the shuffle cuts the deck into blocks and reverses their order, while the cards inside each block keep theirs. Number ten cards 1 to 10 from the top and take blocks of 3, 2, 1 and the remaining 4: you finish with 7 8 9 10, then 6, then 4 5, then 1 2 3. Cards such as 7 and 8 stay neighbours unless a block boundary falls between them, which is why a single overhand shuffle is gentle on a key-card pair.

The riffle shuffle is different. You cut the deck about in half and let the corners of the two halves spring together, so the packets interleave like a zip. Each half keeps its own order, but neighbours are usually parted. Bayer and Diaconis open their famous paper by calling the dovetail, or riffle, shuffle the most commonly used method of shuffling cards.2 Keep two pictures in your head: the overhand moves blocks, the riffle interleaves.

concepts.title: The method: Shuffled Prediction
concepts.contentHtml:
You shuffle in front of the spectator for the whole of a performance, so make it dull. Practise the overhand until your hands do it while you talk: packets of three to eight cards, a steady rhythm, eyes on the spectator, hands low and small. For the riffle, hold a half in each hand with the inner corners touching, let cards fall from both thumbs a few at a time rather than one by one, then push the halves together and square the deck. A good riffle is quiet and slightly ragged. Then use the shuffles in this short trick.

  1. Their shuffle. Hand over the deck face down and say "Shuffle as much as you like." Take it back.
  2. Glimpse. Square the deck, tipping the near end up for a second, and read the bottom card, say the 9♦ (you practised this in The Key Card).
  3. Predict. Write "9♦" on a slip, fold it and leave it in view. Say "I will predict the top card, then shuffle the deck again myself."
  4. Relaxed overhand. Hold the deck face down in your right hand, fingers at the far end and thumb at the near end, above your left palm. Your left thumb pulls packets off the top, which fall into the left hand. Keep talking.
  5. The last card. When a few cards remain in your right hand, pull them off one at a time until a single card is left. That is the old bottom card, the 9♦. Drop it last; it lands on top.
  6. Reveal. Put the deck on the table. Ask them to unfold the slip and read it aloud, then to turn over the top card themselves.

Check it with ten cards: blocks of 3, 4 and 2 leave one card in your hand, and the shuffle gives 10 8 9 4 5 6 7 1 2 3, so the old bottom card is on top. What they see: two fair shuffles and a prediction written before your shuffle. What you do: read one card and let the overhand carry it up. Common mistakes: holding the tip too long, shuffling faster than you talk, and finishing with a riffle, which would part the card from the top.

concepts.title: Myth check: a few overhands mix the deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A handful of overhand shuffles leaves a deck thoroughly mixed.
Reality The overhand shuffle is a slow mixer. Johan Jonasson showed in 2006 that the number of overhand shuffles needed grows roughly as the square of the number of cards, with a logarithm on top.1

Why is it so slow? Recall what one overhand shuffle does: it cuts the deck into blocks and reverses their order. Most neighbouring cards are never separated at all, and a card near the middle travels only a short way. Even many shuffles leave long runs of cards that were together at the start, just in different places. The proof gives a growth rate, not an exact count for 52 cards, but a square law is a different league from the riffle shuffle, which the last lessons of this skill measure.

Wait, really? Jonasson opens his abstract by noting that the overhand is one of the "real" shuffles, since some people actually use it to mix a deck. They are doing something much weaker than they think. For a magician that is good news twice over. An honest-looking overhand moves blocks and leaves the order largely intact, so it is a safe cover for the small controls you meet next.

title: The Jog Control
description: A jogged card marks a chosen card through a casual overhand shuffle, then one cut brings it to the top
tryIt: Practise Lost and Found with a friend as the audience, then perform it for one person and ask whether they noticed the jog.

concepts.title: How it works: a jog is a bookmark
concepts.contentHtml:
A spectator takes a card, it goes back into the middle of the deck, and the deck is shuffled in plain sight. How can you know where it is? You mark it. A jog is a card thrown slightly out of line, so that it sticks out a little from the squared deck. An injog pokes out toward you; an outjog pokes out away from you. Either way it is a bookmark that costs nothing to make, and to anyone watching it looks like a slightly untidy shuffle.

Recall the overhand shuffle: every new packet lands on top. Suppose you shuffle a few packets into your left hand, the spectator puts their card on that pile, and you throw one injogged card on top of it. You then shuffle the rest of the deck over the top. The card directly under the jog is theirs, and the jog is the marker. Lift the jogged card and everything above it, and put that block on the bottom. That is a real cut, made at the place you marked, and it leaves their card on top.

Notice what is honest here. Everything above their card has been genuinely shuffled; only the control is a cut, and as you learned in The Key Card, a cut never parts neighbours. The idea is old. In 1584 Scot told his readers to throw the bottom card, with as many more as they wanted to preserve, a little before or behind the rest.1 That is a jog by another name: a kept card pushed out of line so that the finger can find it.

concepts.title: The method: Lost and Found
concepts.contentHtml:
This control belongs in a performance. You will use it for a trick the spectator sees revealed, and it has no place in a real game. Practise it until the jog is a centimetre, no more, and your eyes never go near it.

  1. Choice. Spread the deck face down and let the spectator take any card, look at it and remember it. Square the deck in your right hand, ready to overhand shuffle.
  2. Start the shuffle. Pull a few packets off the top into your left hand, five to ten cards in all, without ceremony.
  3. Their card goes in. Hold your left hand out: "Put it here, face down." Their card lands on the packet.
  4. The jog. Pull one card off the top of the right-hand deck and drop it on their card, pushed in about a centimetre toward you.
  5. Bury it. Shuffle off the rest in packets, thrown square on top. Keep talking and do not look at the jog.
  6. The cut. With your right hand, lift the jogged card and everything above it as one block, and put it under the cards that remain. Their card is on top.
  7. Reveal. Ask them to name the card, deal the top card face down and turn it over.

Check it with ten numbered cards. Shuffle off 1 2, then 3: the pile reads 3 1 2. Their card C goes on, then the jog, the card 4, then the rest in blocks 5 6 7 and 8 9 10. The pile now reads 8 9 10 5 6 7 4 C 3 1 2. Lift the 4 and everything above it, and put it underneath: C 3 1 2 8 9 10 5 6 7 4. C is on top. What they see: their card lost in an ordinary shuffle. What you do: one jogged card and one cut. Common mistakes: a jog so large it draws the eye, throwing the jog before their card lands, and speeding up at the cut.

concepts.title: Myth check: controls are invisible moves
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A card control needs a secret move that nobody can possibly see.
Reality Nothing in the jog control is hidden. Everyone can see a shuffle, a card dropped on the pile and a cut. The only secret is which card sits under the jog.

That is the pattern in most good card magic. The method is a plain action, performed at a moment when nobody has a reason to wonder about it. A cut after a shuffle is not suspicious, because people cut after shuffling. Where a move would stand out, attention is steered away from it by talk, by timing and by what the performer seems to care about. Misdirection gets its own skill later in this course.

Wait, really? Scot gave advice on exactly this in 1584. For a shuffle that has to hide something, he told readers to begin the shuffle by taking packets as thick as they could,1 so that it looks bold and open, and to leave the fine work for the end. A practical rule follows: start with big, careless blocks, and keep the delicate part, the jog, small and late. Four centuries on, the rhythm of an ordinary shuffle is still hard to beat as cover.

title: False Shuffles and a False Cut
description: Look like you mix while the order stays: a riffle that keeps the top and a cut that changes nothing
tryIt: Practise the false riffle until the last-to-fall rule is automatic, and the three-pile cut until it takes five seconds, then perform Lost and Found in full for one person.

concepts.title: How it works: keep what matters, shuffle the rest
concepts.contentHtml:
A false shuffle looks and sounds like a shuffle but leaves some cards where you put them. It is not a mystery; it is a real shuffle in which you decide which cards fall when. Think of the deck as a top stock, the few cards you want to keep, and everything else.

The overhand shuffle is a poor tool for this, because every packet lands on top and so the top of the deck is always the first thing to move. The riffle is cleaner. When you riffle, the cards of each packet fall from the bottom upward, so the cards that fall first end at the bottom of the merged deck and the cards that fall last end on top. If the last cards to fall all come from the packet that was on top, they keep their place and their order. Take eight cards, with 1 to 4 in the top half and 5 to 8 in the bottom half. Let the cards fall in the order 8, 4, 7, 3, 6, 5, 2, 1. The merged deck reads 1 2 5 6 3 7 4 8 from the top. The cards 1 and 2 have not moved, yet the shuffle looked complete.

A false cut applies the same idea on a larger scale. A true cut moves a block from the top to the bottom, so to fake one you must put the blocks back in their original order, using moves that look as if they could mix anything. Nothing here is for use at a real game: these are shows for a spectator who will see the effect revealed, and nobody respects a performer who borrows them for anything else.

concepts.title: The method: the false riffle and the three-pile cut
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with their card on top, as you left it in Lost and Found. These two moves, done one after the other, convince most people that the card is hopelessly lost, while it has not moved at all.

  1. Cut for the riffle. Lift off roughly half the deck. The half you lifted is the top half, and their card is on its top. Keep track of it.
  2. Riffle. Let the corners spring together, a few cards from each thumb, as in a real shuffle. Near the end, let the bottom half run out first, so that the last cards to fall come from the top half. Square up.
  3. Lay out three piles. Put the deck on the table. Lift off the top third and put it in the centre. Lift off the next third and put it to the left of that. Put the last third to the right of the centre pile.
  4. Collect. Pick up the centre pile and drop it on the left pile. Pick up both and drop them on the right pile.
  5. Reveal. Ask the spectator to name their card, and turn over the top card of the deck.

Check the cut with nine cards. The thirds are 1 2 3, 4 5 6 and 7 8 9. The layout is 4 5 6 on the left, 1 2 3 in the centre and 7 8 9 on the right. The centre goes on the left: 1 2 3 4 5 6. Both go on the right: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9, the original order. What they see: a thorough shuffle and a deck cut into three and reassembled. What you do: keep the last-to-fall cards on top, then undo your own cut. Common mistakes: a riffle that is too neat, cutting thirds that are exactly equal, and glancing at the top card.

concepts.title: Myth check: a false shuffle must be flashy
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A false shuffle only fools people if it is fast and dazzling.
Reality The best false shuffle is dull. It has the same rhythm, the same sound and the same face as your real shuffle, and the performer is talking about something else.

If you shuffle properly for ten seconds and then do a flashy move, the contrast gives it away, even when no one can say how. That is why you practise the real shuffles in the first lesson before the false ones: the false version must be indistinguishable from the real one, and you can only copy what you know well. In practice, talk is part of the method. Your eyes are on the spectator, your question is about their card, and the shuffle is simply something your hands are doing.

Wait, really? Scot gave the same advice in 1584, in a passage about a delicate move. He told readers to use some speech or other device, and to put the hands with the cards to the edge of the table to hide the action.1 He also said a kept packet could be shuffled often to satisfy the curious beholders.2 Shuffling often, to satisfy onlookers who want to see the deck mixed, is precisely what the false riffle and the false cut give you today.

title: How Many Shuffles?
description: Bayer and Diaconis, the slogan "seven shuffles", what mixed means, and the Premo card trick
tryIt: Set a deck in order, let a friend riffle it twice, push a card in, and practise finding the stray in a spread until you can do it in under a minute.

concepts.title: How it works: what "mixed" means
concepts.contentHtml:
How many riffle shuffles does it take to mix a deck? The question needs two things before it has an answer: a model of how people shuffle, and a yardstick for "mixed". The model is the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds shuffle: cut the deck into two packets at a point chosen as if every card were decided by a coin toss, then drop cards from the packets with chances in proportion to their sizes. Bayer and Diaconis cite experiments showing that this model is a good description of the way real people shuffle real cards.1

The yardstick is the total variation distance. Compare two things: the chance that your shuffled deck lands in some set of orders, and the chance it would if the deck were perfectly random. The distance is the biggest gap you can find between them over all sets of orders. It is 1 when an observer can tell your deck from a random one, and 0 when they cannot. For 52 cards, Bayer and Diaconis computed the distance after each shuffle. It stays essentially at its maximum of 1 up to 5 shuffles, when it begins to decrease sharply by factors of 2 each time.2

Read the chart. After one to four riffles the deck is easy to tell from a random one. After five it is 0.92, after six 0.61, after seven 0.33, after eight 0.17, after ten 0.04. People summarise this as "seven shuffles are enough", and the slogan is a fair reading of the table: by seven the distance has fallen to about a third. But the number is a point on a curve, not a law.

concepts.title: The method: Premo, the shuffle detector
concepts.contentHtml:
Bayer and Diaconis note that the key idea in their analysis, rising sequences, was discovered by magicians Williams and Jordan1 at the beginning of the twentieth century. Take a deck in a known order and number the cards 1 to 52. A rising sequence is a maximal set of consecutive numbers that appear in order in the deck. A riffle cuts the deck into two packets, each of which keeps its order, so one riffle leaves exactly two rising sequences. Each extra riffle roughly doubles the count, up to the capacity of the deck. A card pushed in afterwards belongs to no sequence, and that gives you a way to find it.

  1. Set up. Put the deck in an order you know: the spades from ace to king, then the hearts, clubs and diamonds, all face down, with the A♠ on top. The cards are now numbered 1 to 52.
  2. Their shuffles. Turn away and ask the spectator to riffle shuffle the deck, then riffle shuffle it again. No cuts.
  3. Their card. Ask them to look at the top card, remember it, push it into the middle of the deck, square up and hand the deck back.
  4. Spread. Turn round and spread the deck face up in a long row, left to right.
  5. Hunt. For almost every other card, the card numbered one lower lies somewhere to its left. The stray is different: the card one lower lies to its right, and the card one higher lies to its left. Find that card. (For the A♠ only the second test applies.)
  6. Name it. Announce it. If two candidates remain, ask the spectator to name the suit.

Check the logic on twelve cards. After one riffle the order is 1 7 2 3 8 9 4 10 5 6 11 12. Push the 1 into the middle: 7 2 3 8 9 4 1 10 5 6 11 12. The 1 has its 2 on its left, so the sequence cannot continue from it: the 1 is a sequence of one, alone. A computer simulation of the standard shuffle model finds the stray as the only candidate in about 99 of 100 trials after one riffle, 93 after two and 73 after three. So ask for two. The hard part is reading a spread quickly, and that takes practice.

concepts.title: Myth check: seven shuffles is a law
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Seven shuffles is a law of nature: fewer leave the deck unmixed, and more are wasted.
Reality It is where one curve, drawn with one yardstick, happens to cross a convenient height. At seven shuffles the distance from random is 0.33; at ten it is 0.04. Mixing keeps improving, and "mixed" depends on how finely you measure it.

The curve also shows a cutoff. For four shuffles nothing seems to happen, and then the distance collapses, roughly halving with each further shuffle. That behaviour is typical of shuffling, and it is why a deck can feel mixed long before a statistician agrees. Rising sequences give a neat side-fact: a deck that has had fewer than six riffles cannot be in reverse order, since six shuffles give at most 64 rising sequences and 52 are needed for a fully reversed deck.

Wait, really? Bayer and Diaconis use their card trick to say something about cuts, too. They explain that cuts respect the cyclic order of a deck, so by allowing a spectator to cut as often as desired the performer merely gives up knowing where the loop starts.1 That is the ring picture from The Key Card, from a mathematician's side: cutting never mixes, which is why cuts, not shuffles, belong in a key-card trick.

title: The Perfect Shuffle
description: Faro shuffles as a curiosity: why eight out-faros restore a deck, and Three Shuffles with eight cards
tryIt: Practise the eight-card Three Shuffles until all three weaves are clean, then perform it for one person and ask them to guess how many shuffles it takes.

concepts.title: How it works: the perfect shuffle
concepts.contentHtml:
Cut the deck into two exactly equal halves and weave them so the cards alternate perfectly, one from each half, without a single slip. That is a perfect shuffle, and magicians call it the Faro shuffle. It comes in two forms. In an out-shuffle the top card stays on top and the bottom card stays on the bottom. In an in-shuffle the old top card becomes second and the old bottom card second from the bottom.

Because it is exactly repeatable, it is the opposite of a random shuffle. Number the cards 0 to 51 from the top. Each out-shuffle sends card j to position 2j, taken modulo 51 (card 26 goes to position 52 minus 51, which is 1), and the last card stays. After k out-shuffles the card sits at 2k times j, still modulo 51. All cards return home when 2k leaves remainder 1, and 28 = 256 = 5 × 51 + 1. So eight out-shuffles restore a 52-card deck. Diaconis, Graham and Kantor state it directly: a pack of 52 cards requires 8 out shuffles or 52 in shuffles to recycle.1

Magicians met the idea early. The shuffle was introduced to magicians in a brief note in C. T. Jordan's Thirty Card Mysteries, published in 1919.2 The trick there used a smaller packet, and the arithmetic is the same, with a different number: 16 cards return after 4 out-shuffles, 32 after 5, and 8 cards after only 3.

concepts.title: The method: Three Shuffles
concepts.contentHtml:
You do not need a full deck to feel the Faro. Start with eight cards, because they are forgiving, and the result is a small miracle: three perfect shuffles undo themselves.

  1. Show. Lay the A♥ to 8♥ face up in order and let a spectator check. Turn the packet face down with the ace on top.
  2. Split. Cut it exactly in half: the top four (A 2 3 4) in one hand and the bottom four (5 6 7 8) in the other.
  3. First shuffle. Press the inner corners of the halves together and let them spring into one another so the cards alternate one, one. The ace stays on top. The packet reads A 5 2 6 3 7 4 8.
  4. Second shuffle. Split in half again and repeat. The packet reads A 3 5 7 2 4 6 8.
  5. Third shuffle. Once more. The packet reads A 2 3 4 5 6 7 8.
  6. Reveal. Turn the packet face up and spread it: the cards are back in order.

What they see: an ordinary-looking mixing, three times over. What you do: split exactly and weave exactly. Common mistakes: halves that differ by a card, which ruins the order, and letting two cards fall together. Once eight is easy, try sixteen (four shuffles), then thirty-two (five), and only then a full deck, with 26 cards in each half and eight shuffles. In-shuffles would need six for eight cards. A perfect shuffle is a skill of fine control, and it is a curiosity for most magicians, not an everyday tool.

concepts.title: Myth check: perfect means best
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A perfect shuffle must be the best possible shuffle, since it is perfect.
Reality It is the least random shuffle there is. Perfect only means perfectly regular. The same cards go to the same places every time, which is why eight of them restore the deck.

A good mixing shuffle needs chance; a Faro shuffle has none. This is also why it is so useful to a performer. Because it is a fixed rearrangement, you can predict where every card goes. In 1957 Alex Elmsley worked out a binary procedure for bringing the top card to any position.1 Write the number of cards you want above it in binary, and read the digits from the left: a 1 means an in-shuffle and a 0 an out-shuffle. For nine cards above the top card, 9 = 1001, so you give an in-shuffle, two out-shuffles and another in-shuffle, and the top card is tenth from the top. The rule works for every position in a 52-card deck.

Wait, really? The mathematics of Faro shuffles owes much to a rancher. Fred Black, of Thedford, Nebraska, worked out the effect of repeated out-shuffles of 52 cards in some detail, and we know it through the letters of the performer T. Nelson Downs, who reported meetings with him in 1924. Dai Vernon knew Black and said that he used to practise shuffling on horseback.2
